prize_parts.citation: for showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting shape the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extensions changed what a trade model explains: why only some firms export, why liberalisation reallocates activity across firms, and why gains from trade run through productivity selection. The contribution has the combination I weigh most heavily, an explanatory framework together with new empirical data. The framework gave firm-level and customs data a clear structure, and it generated testable predictions that were tested across many countries over more than two decades. The core qualitative predictions have largely held up, and the framework is now standard in graduate training and policy analysis. Krugman's 2008 prize covered earlier new trade theory, so this is a distinct advance. The Melitz-Helpman pairing is also one of the cleaner attribution structures on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: Credit is not fully separable. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum developed closely parallel firm-level trade work but are not on this ballot, and Redding's quantitative extensions are a later strand that a two-name citation leaves out. Some welfare and gains-from-trade magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity. A committee could also judge that trade has been recognised recently enough, in 2008, to favour another field.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B048 first because the framework changed how trade is modelled and produced testable predictions. She ranks B001 only seventh because its influence exceeds the strength of its causal evidence, and she cites the measurement and coding critiques of the legal-origins indices.
responses.response: I agree, and her point moves my own ordering. I ranked B001 first for its combination of new cross-country data and an explanatory structure. But the identification problem is larger than I weighed in my opening: legal origin may proxy for deeper historical and institutional differences, and the coding of the indices is contestable. The firm-heterogeneity predictions have been tested against micro-data in many countries. I now treat that difference in evidentiary robustness as decisive between the two, though B001 remains close.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B001 first because the law-and-finance paradigm reaches across corporate finance, comparative law and development. He accepts that the measurement has been criticised but holds that the paradigm's reach is exceptional.
responses.response: Reach and influence are real, and they are why I kept B001 as my first alternative. But influence is not the same as a settled finding. Part of the literature has moved away from the legal-origins hypothesis, and the three-name cap excludes Vishny from the original papers. Stromberg himself notes that Shleifer has separate prize-level work elsewhere, which blurs the boundary of a citation limited to legal origins. Neither of the other two reservations applies as sharply to the Melitz-Helpman credit.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B048 first and treats Melitz and Helpman as the cleanest credit. She regards Redding's quantitative and spatial work as a later, separate strand, and she asks whether Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum or Yeaple should be considered.
responses.response: I share her reading of the attribution and her Redding exclusion, which also matches my opening view. I would sharpen one point. The parallel Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum work is the real vulnerability, because it concerns priority on the empirical foundations and not only a later extension. The cap of three names cannot resolve this. I would draft the citation around the selection mechanism and gains-from-trade framework so that it does not overclaim the empirical firm-level facts.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B015 first for the task-based framework, the education-technology race and the China-shock evidence. He identifies Hanson as the strongest third name and notes that three names cannot cover every strand.
responses.response: I ranked B015 third and still value its credible designs and large policy impact. My reservations remain the overlap with recent prizes on labour markets and technology, and the unsettled magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects. The three-name cap also forces a choice between Katz and Dorn, and credit for the task framework partly belongs to people outside the ballot. I would keep it as an alternative, not as the preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would require the parallel Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum contributions to be credited, which the ballot cannot accommodate.
How far Helpman's credit should rest on this strand compared with his separate work in B026, and how the overlap affects the framing of the citation.
Whether a trade prize this soon after 2008 weighs against the candidate, even though that bears on field balance and not on merit.
How much weight B001 deserves given its influence, relative to unresolved questions about legal-origins causal identification and Vishny's exclusion.
I rely on my own knowledge of these literatures and have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in labour economics and the economics of crime, and my listed co-authors do not appear among the credited names on B048, B001 or B015. I flag possible familiarity bias toward empirical-design arguments.
